owner: make sure you check the lane bc you were sent some things to put into the guide, but i think i already put them in if they were important points
make sure you clear the humanization queue

entries.title: Experience is not its own interpretation
entries.point: A feeling, thought or attraction is real as an experience but doesn't settle who you are or who you love, so give patterns time instead of letting the feeling of the hour or anyone else decide, without throwing such feelings away either.
entries.where: Practicing With Your Little One > What to Make of a Passing Feeling
entries.quote: Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche's pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably

entries.title: Social practice should be reciprocal, not a performance test
entries.point: Dates, confessions and other contact can turn into reassurance-checking when their hidden job is to prove you're lovable or normal; keep the contact, drop the test, and let it go both ways.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > First Social Connections, Done Right
entries.quote: Neither of those approaches are the balance we're seeking, and both are treating the other person like they're your reassurance machine. I'm giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present.

entries.title: Honesty is graded by earned trust
entries.point: Privacy isn't fakery: people earn more of you by how they handle smaller truths and your no, a deep relationship that needs a fake happy self needs more truth or less depth, and acceptance alone doesn't prove love or trust.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
entries.quote: And reaching out doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no.

entries.title: Anxiety can protect without becoming an oracle
entries.point: Anxiety may be trying to protect you without being right about what will happen, so hear it out without obeying it, and never test a prediction past a part's no to touch, sex, going deeper or an altered state.
entries.where: Practicing With Your Little One > Journal With Each Hand > If it's anxiety
entries.quote: Anxiety is often a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming, like that people will laugh at you. Sometimes it's right, sometimes it's useful, sometimes it's not.
entries.missing: That a part's no, or even hesitation, about sex, going deeper or an altered state is a stop and not a prediction to test; only touch is left ("if you don't want to be touched, say no now", under What to Make of a Passing Feeling). The subsection that said it is his cut X8 (Hear the Guard First's "If it says no, I'd listen" went with X1 too).
entries.basis: The rest went with a passage he cut on purpose (KEEP-AS-IS.json X8).

entries.title: Match outcome claims to duration
entries.point: Relief that fades and comes back is brief relief, not resolution or proof of what worked, and any tracking of it stays light enough not to become checking.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
entries.quote: Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy.
entries.missing: The rule itself: a few hours of relief with the old feeling back later is relief, not a fix or proof of what worked, tracked lightly (jot what changed and how long it lasted, drop it if it feeds OCD patterns); that was If the relief doesn't last, his cut X10. The guide keeps only that calm is initial progress and, for pain, that a treatment that helps doesn't explain the cause.
entries.basis: The rest went with a passage he cut on purpose (KEEP-AS-IS.json X10).

entries.title: Psychoactive adverse history changes planning
entries.point: One psychotic-type or lasting bad reaction to a substance is enough to hold off retrying it until it's properly assessed and to be careful with similar drugs, without becoming an anti-drug rule or a reason to stop prescribed or dependence-forming drugs abruptly.
entries.where: Altered States and Intensive Practice > When Escape Leaves Reality Behind > If a past trip went badly
entries.quote: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don't try again until you understand what would make it safe.

entries.title: A healthy mind is not a perfectly clean mind
entries.point: Unwanted, shameful or contradictory thoughts can come up without being your intent or identity; notice them, act on what you'd stand behind and let the rest go, as Buddhist training works by intention and repair rather than purity.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
entries.quote: Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too. The Guide doesn't need to police your every thought. It notices the jingle and knows you didn't mean it, and that it isn't who you are.

entries.title: Missing can become an optional cue for love
entries.point: Missing someone can, if you like, become a cue for love or loving-kindness, without pushing grief away, assuming they receive it, or using it instead of contact, boundaries or action.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun > Missing Someone
entries.quote: When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn't have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won't help.

entries.title: Concentrated borrowed adulthood can be distributed
entries.point: When one person carries many grown-up jobs for you, sort out which can become yours, which can be spread across people, services, routines or tools, and which belong in that relationship, without weakening a relationship you treasure.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life
entries.quote: it might be mostly one person carrying a lot of it. Maybe you're picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you're struggling can be an enormous blessing. If it's more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn't feel as deep.
entries.missing: The inventory of what that one person carries: which jobs can become yours, which can go to friends, community, services, routines or tools, and which belong in the relationship, and the difference between missing them and practical collapse without them. His reorganization cut the sentence that carried the spreading ("Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works."); it isn't on the keep-as-is list.
entries.basis: The rest went in his own edit inside the paragraph (his sentence "Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works."), which no card asked him to confirm; asked in turn 120, my recommendation: leave it out, since the core point is there in his words.

entries.title: Speak toward what is being built
entries.point: Once reality is named honestly, aim your words at what you're building rather than at a feared identity you're denying, without glossing over grief, harm, anger, a no or who's responsible.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Speak Toward What You Are Building
entries.quote: They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that's something you'd like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself "I'm not dependent." Well, now you're thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant.

entries.title: Clarify support mode only when genuinely ambiguous
entries.point: Listening, helping untangle, brainstorming or a mix are different kinds of support, so ask which is wanted when it's genuinely unclear, without making the question a ritual.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Ask What Kind of Company They Want
entries.quote: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, brainstorm, or...?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it's obvious what they want.

entries.title: Make the opening map explicitly leave the exercise
entries.point: Each stage has to leave the exercise sooner or later: the inner adult becomes believable by starting to give the same care, protection or guidance in ordinary life, even in small ways.
entries.where: Understanding Reparenting > Five Stages of Reparenting
entries.quote: Whichever stage you're at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life.

entries.title: Add the transfer mismatch under “When to Change the Strategy”
entries.point: If the exercise goes well and ordinary life stays the same, the missing step may be transfer rather than a deeper meditation: notice what the adult did in there and do a small piece of it in daily life, without making it homework or a verdict.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
entries.quote: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion.
entries.missing: The mismatch under When to Change the Strategy: a session can go well while life stays the same, which points to a missing transfer step rather than a failed or too-shallow meditation (notice what the adult did in there, do a small piece of it out here), with its limits (no homework after every session; weak carryover isn't proof it was fake). Its last trace there, "integrating the benefits into regular life (like texting a friend...)", was in X10.
entries.basis: The rest went with a passage he cut on purpose (KEEP-AS-IS.json X10).

entries.title: Some real problems are blocked, not actionable yet
entries.point: When every next step on a real problem is blocked by something outside you, waiting isn't avoidance; keep the condition that would reopen it in view and put your effort elsewhere instead of forcing a workaround.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
entries.quote: Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else's end (you've asked, and followed up, and there's nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn't avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

entries.title: Remember a stated support mode and avoid stale advice
entries.point: Remember the kind of support someone said they want until they change it instead of re-asking (and don't guess it from stereotypes), and don't serve advice already given as if it were new.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Ask What Kind of Company They Want
entries.quote: Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it's obvious what they want. But as they say, "assume" makes an "ass" out of "u" and "me."
entries.missing: Remembering the kind of support someone asked for until they change it, not guessing it from gender or another stereotype, and the stale-advice rule (advice already given, with nothing new changing it, gets a brief mention, not a re-run). He removed that paragraph in turn 106 ("it seemed extra"), before the keep-as-is list existed.
entries.basis: The rest went when he removed its paragraph himself in turn 106 ("it seemed extra"); left out, his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Memory support is not the same as reflective journaling
entries.point: When reflective journaling makes things more confusing, a plain record (a dated note, what helped, a reminder, a next step, a voice note) keeps continuity without interpreting, and patterns can wait until later if they matter.
entries.where: Practicing With Your Little One > Journal With Each Hand
entries.quote: For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written. Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.
entries.missing: What the record can be (a dated note of what happened or what helped, a reminder, a next step, a voice note) and that a memory aid doesn't have to explain your life; those sentences went in his reorganization and aren't on the keep-as-is list.
entries.basis: The rest went in his own edit inside the paragraph (what a memory aid can be, and that it needn't explain your life), which no card asked him to confirm; asked in turn 120, my recommendation: leave it out, since the core point is there in his words.

entries.title: One blocked problem should not block the whole life
entries.point: One blocked problem shouldn't stall another that can move: choose the current focus by goal, impact, urgency and what can move now, and when everything feels scrambled, cut it to one organizing statement and one next step.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
entries.quote: The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.
entries.missing: Choosing the current focus by goal, impact, urgency, leverage and what can move now (the guide has only "the next sane step that fits your values"), and the overwhelm rule: one short organizing statement, one prioritized next step, and only a question whose answer would change it.
entries.basis: The rest was never written into the guide (turn 71 counted this entry in with PGQ-014); I'd leave it out, his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Gentler depth without technique-hopping
entries.point: If going deeper is too much, take a gentler step in the same caring relationship rather than switching to another intense technique to prove you can take it.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
entries.quote: Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there's a grown-up around who can say, "Okay, that's enough for today,"

entries.title: Come outward before re-entering
entries.point: If you can't stop and return, or going in keeps making things worse, come all the way back to the room first and return later when comfortable.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
entries.quote: So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can't, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I'd come all the way back out first.

entries.title: A paused practice has a remembered starting point
entries.point: When you pause child contact, note what prompted it and how far you had got, and restart at that level or gentler.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
entries.quote: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far. Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.
entries.missing: The guide has the written reason and progress and a later return once the reason has changed, but never says to resume from that recorded level or gentler (not at full depth).
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Difficulty and harm differ
entries.point: A hard session is not automatically harmful and a pleasant one is not automatically safe or enough; judge by willingness and aftereffects.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
entries.quote: It's a bit like going to the gym. You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.
entries.missing: Says a stormy session can be fine and that you should check willingness and the next days, but never says a pleasant or calming session is not automatically safe or sufficient.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Look at recovery over the next days
entries.point: Judge a session by sleep, ordinary functioning, willingness to return and whether it felt workable, not by how it felt at the time.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
entries.quote: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no?

entries.title: Adapt before escalating
entries.point: If the effect is unclear, make the next session a little easier and change one thing; if functioning is deteriorating, reduce several demands and get support.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
entries.quote: If you can't quite tell yet what feels different, I'd just make the next session simpler, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference.
entries.missing: The unclear-effect step (simpler session, one change) is there, but not the deteriorating-functioning case: reduce several demands at once and seek appropriate support (the guide only says change course sooner if it is making things worse).
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Dreams are present experience, not reconstructed facts
entries.point: Dreams and imagery can show current needs and feelings but are not evidence that a depicted past event happened.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
entries.quote: Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. Although sometimes dreams can show you real memories and even predict the future on occasion, we need to be careful not to assume that they are doing that each time.

entries.title: Reach toward real human connection
entries.point: If isolation was part of the hurt, reaching toward people now is itself a way of caring for your little one and need not wait until you are healed.
entries.where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
entries.quote: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I'd call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too.

entries.title: More than one safe place to belong
entries.point: Keep good existing relationships while adding other communities, and be wary of any group or person demanding to be your only support.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > People? Where Are the People?
entries.quote: Keep the good people you've already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you. And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support

entries.title: Short relief must not perpetuate severe pain
entries.point: In an unbearable pain episode, urgent medical assessment and possible pain relief are the caring alternative to a quick fix known to make things worse, even if earlier tests found nothing.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > Physical Pain Makes It Harder
entries.quote: the best time to get diagnostics done could be right at the actual time of the crisis, rather than waiting until you feel well enough to make an appointment, and they may be able to treat it while it's happening.
entries.missing: Names the harmful quick fix and says crisis-time diagnostics may bring treatment, but never ties these together as the alternative to repeating the known-worse self-medication, nor says to contact urgent medical services for relief during the episode.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Support is not a shortcut to romantic intimacy
entries.point: Friendship and steady support can grow while romance waits; romance comes from mutual love and does not rescue you or reward healing, though you need not be fully healed first.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Dating While You Heal
entries.quote: That doesn't mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won't rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing

entries.title: A chronic pain pathway, not daily emergency calls
entries.point: Frequent severe pain needs an ongoing specialist pathway and a written flare plan with the ER as backup; normal tests do not make the pain imaginary.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > Physical Pain Makes It Harder
entries.quote: I'd ask for a chronic pain specialist and a written plan for the flare-ups you can see coming, including the new or severe signs that mean you go to the ER right away

entries.title: Protective medical agency after coercive or harmful care
entries.point: After harmful or coercive care, choose whom to approach and what to share, favoring trusted voluntary support and a chosen advocate over default family or repeat psychiatric routes, while real imminent danger still gets immediate protection.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Being Your Own Advocate With Doctors
entries.quote: If you don't feel up to it, bring someone you trust to speak up for you (like, not that relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment's for.
entries.missing: Has the chosen advocate and not defaulting to a disrespectful relative, but not that past harmful or coercive treatment changes whom to approach and what to disclose, nor the warning against returning to the same psychiatric pathway or presenting pain-triggered passing thoughts as a plan or bargaining chip.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Gratitude is essential ongoing cultivation; the child is not required to perform it
entries.point: Gratitude, from small goods through suffering itself, is an ongoing essential practice felt as heart-softening (not positive reframing), then used to invite the little one in, without forcing it or excusing harm.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
entries.quote: Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it's essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.

entries.title: A drug peak that changes nothing
entries.point: A drug peak reached while holding every attachment and the anger is not the unconditional love the practice aims at; ask whether anything was let go.
entries.where: Altered States and Intensive Practice > What to Do With a Peak
entries.quote: I'd prefer to ask if any of the discontent has been let go, or the anger? If not, that peak was less the love we're after here than "I'll be grateful once I've got it all,"

entries.title: "If only I had X"
entries.point: Gratitude that waits for conditions never arrives; ask what someone would need before they could feel love or gratitude and whether that list ever ends.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! > Mo' Money, Mo' Problems
entries.quote: Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn't lead to being content with less.
entries.missing: Names conditional gratitude and the endless loop of wanting, but does not offer the question to ask someone who postpones gratitude (what would you need before you could feel it, and does that list ever end).
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Bringing gratitude in without pushing it
entries.point: Offer gratitude sideways and at times, return to it later if resisted, using small concrete questions, and work toward contradictions from the love side.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
entries.quote: Being thankful shouldn't be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment.
entries.missing: Only the not-pushing and the toxic-positivity disclaimer are there. Missing: coming back to it later when resisted, example small questions (smallest part of a better life, moment-by-moment peace, grateful for a past partner), that ignoring every positive is also toxic, and working a contradiction like 'I love everyone, I hate my dad' from the love side.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Gratitude in a calm altered state
entries.point: In a calm, safe, clear altered state gratitude can be practiced as when sober; if overwhelming settle first, and with impaired capacity or a medical concern put safety first.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
entries.quote: On the other hand, I've noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.
entries.missing: Only a personal anecdote of gratitude turning a bad trip. Missing: that gratitude in a calm altered state is practiced as sober, and the conditions: settle first while overwhelmed, safety and care first with impaired capacity or a medical concern.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Hypnosis isn't ruled out by grief or an altered state
entries.point: Hypnosis can suit grieving or altered-state readers depending on type, level of grief and above all purpose (reaching blocked feelings versus escaping), while deep inner-child work waits until grief is less raw.
entries.missing: Nothing on hypnosis during fresh grief or an altered state; the guide only says gentle meditation or self-hypnosis calms the nervous system and is not for all-day coping. Missing: fit depends on kind, grief level and purpose; hypnosis to reach numb feelings can help, to escape is less useful; deep inner-child work waits until grief is less raw.
entries.basis: Left out: the guide never raises whether hypnosis suits someone grieving, so I recommended leaving it out (turn 119); his reply of 09:42 took the other open item and raised no objection, and at 10:02 he asked for the queue to be cleared.

entries.title: Reparenting is not an exercise
entries.point: Reparenting is the ongoing adult-to-child relationship lived in boundaries and everyday choices, not an exercise to finish; meditations are ways of practicing it, not its measure.
entries.where: Understanding Reparenting > Five Stages of Reparenting
entries.quote: Reparenting isn't an exercise you finish, even if you make excellent progress. You might feel like you've mastered the adult/child inner relationship, and then it's Friday night and your boss asks you to stay late again.

entries.title: Keeping yourself safe is part of the work, not a separate track
entries.point: Everyday protective steps (leaving, resting, boundaries, company) are the adult protecting the child and so are reparenting, while outside help stays its own thing.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
entries.quote: Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector's plain acts and the warmth can come after

entries.title: Before sharing something legally or personally sensitive
entries.point: Before disclosing highly sensitive material, know that digital records persist, some professionals must report, ask what must be reported and documented first, and still disclose current danger.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace > Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
entries.quote: So I'd ask this person, before handing over any tricky specifics: "What does the law require you to report?" That's a normal and expected question.
entries.missing: Missing: asking what gets documented and who can access records; legal privilege versus professional confidentiality; seeking qualified legal advice for legal exposure; AI chats and apps as a retained medium. The guide also says it wouldn't bother asking, and suggests recasting as a dream narrative.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Ask what help could actually change, and what a practice actually did
entries.point: After repeated failed care tie a new referral to a specific benefit, learn how a helpful practice worked before warning, keep dreams apart from waking testimony, treat relapse as changed conditions, and don't take coaching support as proof a product works.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
entries.quote: Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself, "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?"
entries.missing: Has asking what a practice is for and whether it helps, and caution about dreams and vivid memories elsewhere. Missing: tying a further non-urgent referral to a specific benefit or different expertise, learning how a practice that helped affected the person and its drawbacks, reading a relapse after long improvement as changed conditions rather than shame, and that a coach's personal support is not proof a product works.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Make existing partial regulation usable outside the exercise
entries.point: A small release of body tension doesn't prove anxiety is gone; notice the specific effect, whether continuing changes it, how long it lasts and what carries into life, and keep a tiny list of tested supports when overwhelmed.
entries.where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
entries.quote: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship.
entries.missing: Has carry-over to daily life as the test and that calmer feelings alone are only initial progress. Missing: that a small bodily release doesn't prove the whole anxiety state is gone; noticing specific effect, effect of continuing and how long benefit lasts; keeping a tiny list of already-tested accessible supports when overwhelmed.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Protect from relapse by understanding the need, not repeating how to stop
entries.point: Stopping a harmful coping habit differs from not resuming it under distress; ask what it supplies at the critical moment, what non-harmful experiences can meet part of that, and whether a protective step reduces access.
entries.where: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns > How Distrust Reproduces
entries.quote: With any of these patterns, I'd ask what it's protecting you from, because it doesn't really help to just label it a bad habit.
entries.missing: Has asking what a coping pattern is protecting you from. Missing: the distinction between being able to stop and avoiding resuming under distress, finding already-known non-harmful experiences that meet part of the need, and a low-friction step that reduces real-world access (without promises or coercive relocation).
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Notice feelings, choose actions without self-condemnation
entries.point: A feeling can arise unchosen; examine it kindly and decline to act when it conflicts with consent, safety or a trusted boundary, which is self-protection, not a defect.
entries.where: Practicing With Your Little One > What to Make of a Passing Feeling
entries.quote: "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love.
entries.missing: Has feelings not defining you and unwanted thoughts not making you bad (funeral jingle). Missing: deciding not to act on a feeling when it conflicts with consent, safety, vulnerability or a trusted boundary and calling that mature self-protection, separating feelings, intentions, actions and risks, and not inferring the origin of an attraction from unverified memories or promising a cure.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Shame appraisal, realistic repair and selective belonging
entries.point: Separate social rejection from moral rightness, initial shame from self-attack, own precise responsibility and possible repair, and consider leaving groups that repeatedly reject you unjustly.
entries.where: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns > How to Forgive Without Forgetting > Forgiving Yourself
entries.quote: Own what you did (only what was really yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends, and by changing behavior going forward.
entries.missing: Responsibility, repair, ashamed-of-being-ashamed, shame as a signal versus intrusive-thought shame, pressured forgiveness, belonging bargains and breaks from groups are scattered across sections. Not stated: that actual or feared social rejection is a separate question from whether you were morally wrong, and the instruction not to prescribe disclosure to unpredictable or hostile audiences or to split blame numerically.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Choosing whom to tell, and where an AI helper stops
entries.point: Choose a confidant by ease with hard subjects, test with a general version first, ask a therapist what they must report, find an early-sexual-trauma therapist, handle accidental illegal material properly, and know an AI helper has limits.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
entries.quote: People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party
entries.missing: Has earned trust through smaller truths and asking what a professional must report. Missing: choosing the listener by ease with difficult subjects rather than closeness, opening with the general kind of thing and asking if they are open to more, seeking a therapist experienced in early sexual trauma without needing certainty, not saving or sharing illegal material seen by accident, and that an AI helper has limits and should say so.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: Go back over what each person said and did before judging a reaction
entries.point: Before deciding what someone's reaction means, reconstruct in order what each person said and did, including your own words and actions.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
entries.quote: Sometimes folks are shocked at the response they get (why does everyone always reject me?), without even considering whether that response was easily predictable based on the energy they gave out to spark it.
entries.missing: Has weighing your own contribution to a reaction and not judging by one fight. Missing: the step of going back over what each person actually said and did, in order, before deciding what the reaction means.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: How this guide differs from schema therapy
entries.point: The guide keeps three schema-therapy ideas and differs by using the reader's own words rather than schemas, not guessing history from labels, having the reader do the reparenting, not fighting any part, and not claiming schema-therapy research supports it.
entries.where: Conclusion and Appendix > Appendix > Schema Therapy
entries.quote: So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent.
entries.missing: Has the kept ideas, the questionnaire and 18 schemas/modes, history assumed from labels, borrowed adulthood and a note on a more combative stance. Missing: that here you describe parts in your own words and your history is what you tell; that any helper hands reparenting back; that no part is fought or expelled and a harsh critic's contempt need not be obeyed; and the statement that schema-therapy research does not show this guide works.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: After a painful disagreement, ask what you aimed for, what you expected and how you judge it now
entries.point: Looking back on a hurtful disagreement, set side by side your aim, expected response and present judgment; you can stand by your view, wish you'd said it differently and accept a consequence.
entries.where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
entries.quote: Be honest with yourself about what your goal is for this communication. Do you want to break someone mighty down? To show that you or your views matter? Or do you want them to listen and hear you without getting defensive?
entries.missing: The aim question is asked before sending. Missing: the retrospective look at what you aimed for, what response you expected and how you now judge what you said and what followed, and that standing by a conviction, wishing you had expressed it differently and accepting a foreseen consequence can all be true.
entries.basis: The rest left out, as I recommended in turn 119; his call (00:56 and 10:02 UTC).

entries.title: A critical voice is not automatically a protector, and you can reject the insult without first settling what it is
entries.point: A harsh inner voice may be a learned script, a protector, a cruel real point or a mix; meet it with compassion and firm limits and refuse the contempt without first deciding which.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One > Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
entries.quote: critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.

entries.title: Proactive protection includes a self-critical strategy that is trying to prevent a feared outcome, not every inner critic
entries.point: A self-critical voice counts as protection only when it is working to prevent a feared outcome; an inner critic is not a guard by default.
entries.where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One > Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
entries.quote: it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.

entries.title: If anger is hard to put into words, try drawing or scribbling it
entries.point: If anger is hard to word, draw or scribble it without making anything recognizable, then see whether a feeling, need, boundary or action has become clearer.
entries.where: Practicing With Your Little One > Journal With Each Hand
entries.quote: A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it's had its say, even if all it can do is scribble angrily.
entries.basis: His own line of 2026-11-04 09:42 UTC (experiments/t120-answers/JOEL-20261104-0942.md).

entries.title: A deeper spiritual level can bring release, love and reassurance, but is not a source of facts about ordinary life and does not replace discernment
entries.point: A deeper level of wisdom and compassion can bring love and peace, but isn't treated as a source of specific facts or a replacement for discernment.
entries.where: Conclusion and Appendix > Appendix > Internal Family Systems (IFS)
entries.quote: though it can still give the same love, peace, and clarity to whomever accesses it. Where I part ways with IFS is I don't think the Higher Self has any *specific* wisdom that can be followed mechanically.
